title: Mathematical Basis of Stability Analysis
markdown: ## What this covers This lecture does two things that only make sense read together. First, it recaps a piece of mathematical machinery — nullclines, linearization, the Jacobian, and the trace/determinant criterion for a two-variable system — that the course has already been using to decide whether a fixed point of a genetic switch is stable. Second, it opens a new case study, the chemotactic signaling pathway of *E. coli*, and spends most of its time laying out the phenomenon: what the pathway does, what it is built from, and the quantitative properties (gain, sensitivity, perfect adaptation, robustness) that a model of it will be judged against. The modeling itself — turning the pathway into equations and analyzing them with the tool in the first half — is left for the next lecture; what is given here is the toolkit and the assumptions the model will use. It assumes you already have fixed points of two-variable ODE systems, and have seen the two preceding lectures on genetic switches (the lysis–lysogeny decision, the engineered genetic toggle switch), since the stability question this lecture answers is the same one those switches raised. ## The stability-analysis toolkit for two-variable systems Take any system of two coupled, generally nonlinear, ODEs, $$\dot x = f(x,y), \qquad \dot y = g(x,y).$$ Six steps decide whether a fixed point of this system is stable. **Step 1 — find the fixed points.** Set $\dot x = 0$ and $\dot y = 0$ simultaneously: a fixed point $(x_o,y_o)$ satisfies $f(x_o,y_o)=0$ and $g(x_o,y_o)=0$. (Plotting the two curves $f=0$ and $g=0$ — the nullclines — and reading off their intersections is the usual way to find these.) **Step 2 — look at a small deviation from the fixed point.** Define $\tilde x \equiv x - x_o$ and $\tilde y \equiv y - y_o$. Near the fixed point these are small, and the question of stability is exactly the question of what $\tilde x(t), \tilde y(t)$ do as $t \to \infty$. **Step 3 — linearize.** Taylor-expand $f$ and $g$ to first order about $(x_o,y_o)$ and drop the higher-order terms (justified because $\tilde x, \tilde y$ are small): $$\dot x \approx \tilde x \left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{(x_o,y_o)} + \tilde y \left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right|_{(x_o,y_o)} \equiv a\tilde x + b\tilde y,$$ $$\dot y \approx \tilde x \left.\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\right|_{(x_o,y_o)} + \tilde y \left.\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\right|_{(x_o,y_o)} \equiv c\tilde x + d\tilde y.$$ Since $x_o, y_o$ are constant, $\dot{\tilde x} = \dot x$ and $\dot{\tilde y} = \dot y$, so this is a *linear* system for $\tilde x, \tilde y$ — the nonlinear problem has been replaced, near the fixed point only, by a linear one that can be solved in closed form. **Step 4 — write down the Jacobian.** Collect the four partial derivatives into the matrix $$A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}.$$ **Step 5 — take its trace and determinant.** $$\tau = \mathrm{tr}(A) = a+d, \qquad \Delta = \det(A) = ad-bc.$$ **Step 6 — read off stability.** $(x_o,y_o)$ is a stable fixed point if and only if $\tau<0$ and $\Delta>0$. That last line is stated as a rule on the slide, but it is worth seeing why it is true, because the "why" is what tells you it stops working outside two dimensions. A linear system $\dot{\tilde x}=A\tilde x$ decays to zero exactly when every eigenvalue of $A$ has negative real part. For a $2\times2$ matrix the eigenvalues solve the characteristic equation $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$, which works out to $$\lambda^2 - \tau\lambda + \Delta = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda_{1,2} = \frac{\tau \pm \sqrt{\tau^2-4\Delta}}{2}.$$ Two facts about a quadratic's roots do all the work: the roots multiply to $\Delta$ and add to $\tau$. - If $\Delta<0$, the roots are real (the discriminant $\tau^2-4\Delta$ is then a sum of two positive numbers) and, multiplying to a negative number, have opposite sign. One eigenvalue is positive, so the fixed point is a saddle — unstable along one direction no matter what $\tau$ is. - If $\Delta>0$, the two eigenvalues share a sign. When $\tau^2\geq4\Delta$ they are real, and since they add to $\tau$, that shared sign is the sign of $\tau$: both negative (stable node) if $\tau<0$, both positive (unstable node) if $\tau>0$. When $\tau^2<4\Delta$ they are a complex conjugate pair with real part exactly $\tau/2$: a decaying spiral if $\tau<0$, a growing spiral if $\tau>0$. So $\Delta>0$ and $\tau<0$ is the only combination in which both eigenvalues have negative real part — which is exactly the trace/determinant criterion. The boundary case $\tau=0,\Delta>0$ gives a purely imaginary pair (a center), which the linear approximation cannot classify — you would need to look at the nonlinear terms it dropped in step 3. The one warning attached to the rule matters as much as the rule: **this criterion is only valid in two dimensions.** In three or more variables the Jacobian has more than two eigenvalues, and the trace and determinant alone no longer pin down the sign of every eigenvalue's real part — you need the full set of eigenvalues, or the more general (and more cumbersome) Routh–Hurwitz conditions. ## Why chemotaxis needs a faster switch The previous two pairs of lectures built genetic switches: the naturally occurring lysis–lysogeny decision, and the engineered genetic toggle switch. Both are examples of a more general need — cells constantly have to make binary decisions: what to become (development and differentiation, e.g. in stem cells), what to eat (metabolism), what to make (e.g. which amino acid to synthesize. A switch built out of gene expression works on a timescale of roughly ten minutes to hours, set by the time it takes to transcribe, translate, and accumulate protein. That is far too slow for some of the decisions a cell has to make — finding food, chasing prey (or avoiding being one), and signal transduction generally, all need a response on a timescale of milliseconds to minutes. The fix is to move the switch down a level: instead of turning genes on and off, flip individual proteins between an active and an inactive state, leaving the total amount of that protein (active plus inactive) fixed and gene expression out of the picture entirely. Such protein switches are usually built from a fast, reversible covalent modification — phosphorylation is the standard example — and that is the level at which the rest of this lecture's system operates. ## The hydrogen atom of signal transduction The example the lecture introduces at this faster timescale is the chemotactic signaling pathway of *Escherichia coli* — a cell about 1–2 $\mu$m long and 0.5 $\mu$m in diameter, swimming by rotating a handful of flagella. Rotating counterclockwise, the flagella bundle into a single helical propeller and the cell swims in a straight "run"; rotating clockwise, the bundle flies apart and the cell "tumbles" in place, picking a new random direction for the next run. In the absence of any chemical attractant this alternation is essentially unbiased, and the result is a random walk. In the presence of an attractant, the pattern of tumbling and running is biased so that the cell drifts up the gradient — and, notably, the gradient is sensed *temporally* rather than spatially: not by comparing concentration across the length of the cell, but from what the cell itself experiences as it swims. This system has been called (in the lecture's own framing) the hydrogen atom of signal transduction — the standard, best-understood minimal example, the one everything else in the subject is checked against — and for good reason: it has been studied for roughly a hundred years (background reading: Alberts et al., *Molecular Biology of the Cell*, 4th ed., ch. 13). ## The chemotactic relay: phosphorylation and methylation The pathway that connects a bound ligand to the flagellar motor is built from two kinds of covalent modification of the same set of proteins, redrawn schematically below after the pathway figure in Falke et al. (1997): - **Phosphorylation** of CheA, CheY, and CheB — fast, and the direct route from receptor occupancy to motor bias. - **Methylation** of the receptor (Tar) by CheR and CheB-P — slow, and the basis of the pathway's adaptation. The kinase **CheA** uses ATP to autophosphorylate one of its own histidines, $\text{CheA} + \text{ATP} \leftrightharpoons \text{CheA}_p + \text{ADP}$. CheA (and CheA$_p$) sit bound to the Tar receptor through the adaptor protein CheW, which itself has no enzymatic activity of its own (CheA/CheW/Tar together are sometimes called a "scaffolding" complex). CheA$_p$ is unstable and passes its phosphate on to the soluble response regulator **CheY**: $\text{CheA}_p + \text{CheY} \leftrightharpoons \text{CheA} + \text{CheY}_p$. CheY$_p$ diffuses through the cytoplasm and binds the motor protein FliM, and binding drives clockwise rotation — tumbling. So the logic is direct: high CheA activity gives high $[\text{CheY}_p]$ and lots of tumbling; low CheA activity gives low $[\text{CheY}_p]$ and straight swimming. The phosphatase **CheZ** runs the reaction the other way, $\text{CheY}_p + \text{CheZ} \leftrightharpoons \text{CheY} + \text{CheZ}_p$, so high CheZ pushes toward low $[\text{CheY}_p]$ and straight swimming as well. The rate at which CheA autophosphorylates is stimulated by *unoccupied* receptors — an attractant binding the receptor lowers CheA's activity, lowers $[\text{CheY}_p]$, and produces the longer runs (less tumbling) that carry the cell up the gradient. That covers excitation — the fast response to a change in occupancy. It is not enough on its own: if CheA's activity simply tracked occupancy, the cell would only ever respond to the very first change in concentration it met and then sit at whatever bias that level demanded, rather than resetting itself to explore further. **Adaptation** closes that gap, on the slower, methylation side of the pathway. CheR constitutively adds methyl groups to the receptor; CheB, only once phosphorylated by CheA into CheB$_p$, removes them again — so the demethylation rate is itself set by CheA's own phosphorylation state, coupling the slow loop back to the fast one. ## What a model of the pathway has to reproduce Before building a model (that is the next lecture's job), the slides walk through what recent experiments had already measured, because these numbers are the target any model has to hit. - **Enormous gain.** Sourjik and Berg used FRET to track CheY$_p$–CheZ binding and receptor occupancy directly in living cells (*PNAS* 99, 123 (2002); *PNAS* 99, 12669 (2002)) and found an amplification of about 35 between receptor occupancy and $[\text{CheY}_p]$, and a further amplification of about 10 between $[\text{CheY}_p]$ and the motor's response — a total gain of roughly 350. The slides flag receptor clustering as the likely source of this amplification, to be picked up when the model is built. - **Very different sensitivities at the two ends.** Sourjik and Berg's receptor-occupancy data give a Hill coefficient of about 1 (occupancy responds roughly hyperbolically to ligand). Cluzel, Surette, and Leibler's single-cell measurements of motor bias against CheY-GFP expression (*Science* 287, 1652 (2000), in a CheY$^-$, CheZ$^-$, CheB$^-$ strain, assuming all CheY present is phosphorylated) give a Hill coefficient of about 10 at the motor — a strongly ultrasensitive switch. - **Perfect adaptation.** The response to a step change in attractant is fast excitation followed by a slow return of $[\text{CheY}_p]$, and hence the tumbling frequency, back to essentially its pre-stimulus value — regardless of the new steady background concentration. This is also what the methylation-versus-behavior correlation shows directly on the slides: adding attractant, adding more, then removing it, tracks with tumbling and (on the slower timescale) with methylation level. *E. coli* senses attractant concentrations from 10 nM up to 1 mM and resolves changes in that concentration as small as 0.1%. - **Robustness of that adaptation.** Alon, Surette, Barkai, and Leibler (*Nature* 397, 168 (1999)) showed that the precision of the adapted (pre-stimulus) tumbling frequency is robust to large changes in the concentrations of the Che proteins themselves — but the slides are explicit that *not all* parameters of the system share this robustness. The Spiro, Parkinson, and Othmer model (*PNAS* 94, 7263 (1997)) is named on the slides as the "fine-tuned model for perfect adaptation," built around the Tar–CheA–CheW complex, and is the model the next lecture develops to try to reproduce this list quantitatively as well as qualitatively. ## Setting up the model: the assumptions The notes list the simplifying assumptions that model is built on, ahead of actually writing down its equations: 1. Tar is the only receptor type considered, and CheW and CheA are always bound to it. 2. Methylation occurs in a specific order (through a fixed sequence of methylation states). 3. Only the three highest methylation states are kept in the model. 4. Only CheB$_p$ (not unphosphorylated CheB) demethylates the receptor. 5. Phosphorylation of CheA does not affect ligand (un)binding. 6. Tar–CheR binding does not affect ligand (un)binding or CheA phosphorylation. 7. CheZ is not itself regulated. 8. Phosphotransfer from the receptor complex to CheY or to CheB is not affected by ligand occupancy or by methylation state. Two further rules, attached to a timescale classification of the receptor's states as fast, slow, or intermediate, are what actually generate adaptation dynamically: ligand-bound receptor states generally have *lower* autophosphorylation rates, and CheR methylates ligand-bound states *more rapidly* than unbound ones. Together these mean that a receptor that stays occupied is driven, over the following minutes, toward higher methylation — but the notes stop short of stating explicitly how that higher methylation state feeds back into raising CheA's activity again. That closing step is presumably exactly what the model built next lecture makes precise. ## Exercises The course's problem set attached to this material has two parts. ### 1. Design principles (22 points) **1.1 Robustness.** Robust timing — this is Uri Alon's Exercise 8.4 (8 points). *(The exercise statement itself is in Alon's textbook and is not reproduced here.)* **1.2 Optimality.** a. Optimal genetic code — Uri Alon's Exercise 9.4 (8 points). b. Fitness function — Uri Alon's Exercises 10.1 and 10.2 (6 points). *(Again, these statements are in the textbook, not in the lecture material supplied here.)* ### 2. The cAMP relay in *Dictyostelium* (28 points) *Dictyostelium* amoebae are free-living cells that, under starvation, aggregate into a single multicellular organism. The process starts when starving amoebae emit pulses of the chemoattractant cAMP, which draws neighboring cells inward and triggers them to secrete cAMP themselves — generating outward-spiraling waves of cAMP that direct the whole population toward the original source. This problem works through the origin of, and the response to, those waves. Two species of cAMP receptor sit in the cell membrane: an "activator" $A$ and an "inhibitor" $I$, both acting on a third protein $R$. A cAMP-bound pair of $A$ molecules catalyzes conversion of $R$ to an active form $R^*$; a cAMP-bound pair of $I$ molecules catalyzes the reverse reaction. **2.1 Chemical kinetics of cAMP signaling (6 points).** a. The initial binding of cAMP ($C$) to its receptors is $$A + C \underset{k_A^-}{\overset{k_A^+}{\rightleftharpoons}} AC, \qquad I + C \underset{k_I^-}{\overset{k_I^+}{\rightleftharpoons}} IC.$$ Write the equations for the time evolution of $[AC]$ and $[IC]$. Assuming $[AC]\ll[A_{\text{tot}}]$ and $[IC]\ll[I_{\text{tot}}]$, and writing $a\propto[AC]$, $i\propto[IC]$, $c\propto[C]$, show that with a convenient choice of units these reduce to $$\frac{da}{dt} = k_A^-(c-a), \qquad \frac{di}{dt} = k_I^-(c-i).$$ b. The activation/inactivation of $R$ reaches rapid equilibrium, $R \underset{k_R^- i^2}{\overset{k_R^+ a^2}{\rightleftharpoons}} R^*$ (the $a^2, i^2$ dependence comes from needing two molecules of $AC$ or $IC$ to catalyze the conversion). Writing $\beta = k_R^-/k_R^+$, find the rapid-equilibrium value of $r=[R^*]$ in terms of $a$, $i$, and $[R_{\text{tot}}]$. **2.2 Positive feedback and oscillations (12 points).** $R^*$ is adenylate cyclase: active, it converts ATP into cytoplasmic cAMP, which is secreted into the environment — a positive feedback loop on extracellular cAMP. Let $c_1=[\text{cAMP}_{\text{in}}]$, let cytoplasmic synthesis proceed at rate $k_1 r$, secretion at rate constant $k_0$, and let phosphodiesterase degrade cAMP with rate constants $\gamma_1$ (inside) and $\gamma_0$ (outside): $$\frac{dc_1}{dt} = k_1 r - (\gamma_1+k_0)c_1, \qquad \frac{dc}{dt} = k_0 c_1 - \gamma_0 c.$$ a. Assuming $c_1$ and $a$ reach rapid equilibrium, reduce the four equations above to two equations for the slow variables $c$ and $i$, of the form $$\frac{dc}{dt} = \frac{c^2}{\beta i^2+c^2} - c, \qquad \frac{di}{dt} = k(c-i).$$ Show the choice of units this requires, and find $k$ in terms of the original rate constants. b. Find the conditions on $k$ and $\beta$ under which this system is oscillatory (i.e. has a limit cycle) — this is exactly the trace/determinant question from earlier in this chapter, applied to a new pair of nullclines. c. **(Computation)** Plot the $i$–$c$ nullclines and simulate the time evolution for an oscillatory case. d. Suppose only a single molecule of $AC$ or $IC$, rather than a pair, were needed to catalyze the $R$ conversion. Comment on how the system's behavior changes. **2.3 Diffusion and cAMP waves (10 points, computation).** On a plate rather than in stirred liquid, cAMP diffuses slowly and its extracellular concentration varies over space as well as time — cells act like an array of transmitters that detect, amplify, and re-broadcast the cAMP signal. In one spatial dimension, with cells uniformly distributed along a line whose positions are fixed on the timescales considered, the system obeys $$\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = \frac{c^2}{\beta i^2+c^2} - c + D\frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial x^2}, \qquad \frac{\partial i}{\partial t} = k(c-i).$$ Write a numerical simulation of this system on $x\in[-1,1]$ with no-flux boundaries, starting from a smooth, localized pulse of cAMP of width $\sigma$ centered at the origin and going to zero at the boundaries, with a uniform initial inhibitor concentration $i_o$. a. Using $\beta=4$, $k=0.5$, $D=10^{-7}$, $\sigma=0.1$, $i_o=0.1$, run the simulation and observe cAMP waves emerging from the origin. Plot a typical profile and indicate the direction the waves travel. b. Re-run with a value of $k$ that makes the system non-oscillatory. Describe the resulting cAMP profile once transients have died out, and say whether a cell could use it to locate the original source of cAMP. ## Sources - **Slides**: `lectures/07-notes/01-mathematical-basis-of-stability-analysis.md`, `02-chemotactic-pathway-in-e-coli.md`, and `03-assumptions.md`, from the 2004 offering of MIT OCW 8.591J/9.531J *Systems Biology*, lecture 7. These carry the stability-analysis recap, the genetic-switch and protein-switch framing, the chemotaxis background (run/tumble motility, temporal gradient sensing), the phosphorylation and methylation pathway description, the experimental gain/sensitivity/adaptation/robustness summary, and the Spiro et al. modeling assumptions. The lecture notes are a model's reconstruction of a PDF with no text layer, flagged by the source itself as unverified equation-by-equation. - **No transcript or spoken narration was supplied for this lecture** — the exposition above is built entirely from the slide notes, without the motivating asides a recording would normally add. - **Exercises**: `psets/07-questions.md`, Problem Set 7 from the 2014 offering of the same course.
